topic: Retirement plans, farmers and rental property

notes.front: What is a simplified employee pension (SEP)?
notes.back: A written plan under which the employer contributes to a SEP IRA set up for each eligible employee, without a more complex qualified plan.
notes.explanation: Contributions go into an individual retirement arrangement set up for each eligible employee.
notes.example: Like paying into each worker’s own IRA on their behalf, under one short written plan, instead of running a pension scheme.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Chapter 2. Simplified Employee Pensions (SEPs)”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: A SEP is a written plan that allows you to make contributions toward your own retirement and your employees' retirement without getting involved in a more complex qualified plan. Under a SEP, you make contributions to an individual retirement arrangement (called a SEP IRA) set up by or for each eligible employee.

notes.front: What is a qualified plan?
notes.back: An employer retirement plan, such as a 401(k), profit-sharing or defined benefit plan, that meets the tax law’s qualification rules to get their tax benefits.
notes.explanation: Meeting the qualification rules is the condition for getting the tax benefits of a qualified plan.
notes.example: Like a company pension scheme that passes an inspection: meet the rules and the tax benefits follow.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Qualification Rules”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: To qualify for the tax benefits available to qualified plans, a plan must meet certain requirements (qualification rules) of the tax law.

notes.front: In Pub 560, what are annual additions?
notes.back: The total of the employer’s contributions for a year, employee contributions (excluding rollovers) and forfeitures allocated to a participant’s account.
notes.explanation: Annual additions are what the defined contribution limit is measured against.
notes.example: Like everything paid into one worker’s pot in a year: the firm’s money, the worker’s own and any forfeited balances shared out.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Chapter 1. Definitions: Annual additions”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Annual additions are the total of all your contributions in a year, employee contributions (not including rollovers), and forfeitures allocated to a participant's account.

notes.front: What is a SIMPLE IRA plan, and which employers may set one up?
notes.back: A salary reduction plan paying into employees’ SIMPLE IRAs, for employers with 100 or fewer employees paid $5,000 or more last year.
notes.explanation: Employees choose salary reduction contributions, and the employer adds matching or nonelective contributions.
notes.example: Like a workplace savings scheme for a small firm: staff divert part of their pay and the firm tops it up.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “SIMPLE Plans”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Generally, if you had 100 or fewer employees who received at least $5,000 in compensation last year, you can set up a SIMPLE IRA plan. Under a SIMPLE plan, employees can choose to make salary reduction contributions rather than receiving these amounts as part of their regular pay. In addition, you will contribute matching or nonelective contributions.

notes.front: What is a catch-up contribution?
notes.back: An extra elective deferral allowed to participants aged 50 or over by the end of the year, above the normal deferral limit ($7,500 for 2025).
notes.explanation: Deferrals count as catch-up only once they exceed the ordinary elective deferral limit.
notes.example: Like an extra allowance for savers in their fifties: they may put in more than younger colleagues.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Catch-up contributions”, PDF p. 12
notes.evidence: A SARSEP can permit participants who are age 50 or over at the end of the calendar year to also make catch-up contributions. The catch-up contribution limit is $7,500 for 2025 and $8,000 for 2026. Elective deferrals aren't treated as catch-up contributions for 2025 until they exceed the elective deferral limit

notes.front: What is a defined benefit plan?
notes.back: Any plan that is not a defined contribution plan; contributions are what is needed to provide definitely determinable benefits.
notes.explanation: Figuring those contributions needs actuarial assumptions and computations, so continuing professional help is generally needed.
notes.example: Like a promised pension of a set amount a year: the employer pays in whatever it takes to fund that promise.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Defined Benefit Plan”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: defined benefit plan is any plan that isn't a defined contribution plan. Contributions to a defined benefit plan are based on what is needed to provide definitely determinable benefits to plan participants. Actuarial assumptions and computations are required to figure these contributions. Generally, you will need continuing professional help to have a defined benefit plan.

notes.front: Who is a highly compensated employee (HCE)?
notes.back: A more-than-5% owner in the year or preceding year, or someone paid over the threshold in the preceding year ($155,000 if that year is 2024).
notes.explanation: Ownership alone is enough, whatever the pay; otherwise the test looks at the preceding year’s compensation.
notes.example: Like the people at the top of the payroll or the share register, whom plan rules must not favour.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Chapter 1. Definitions: Highly compensated employee”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: Owned more than 5% of the interest in your business at any time during the year or the preceding year, regardless of how much compensation that person earned or received; or • For the preceding year, received compensation from you of more than $155,000 (if the preceding year is 2024

notes.front: What is a top-heavy plan?
notes.back: A plan that mainly favours partners, sole proprietors and other key employees, measured by their share of accrued benefits or account balances.
notes.explanation: The label turns on who holds the plan’s value, not on how many people take part.
notes.example: Like a scheme where the owners hold most of the money: special minimums then kick in for everyone else.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Top-heavy plan requirements”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: A top-heavy plan is one that mainly favors partners, sole proprietors, and other key employees.

notes.front: In a retirement plan, what does vesting mean?
notes.back: Gaining a fixed, nonforfeitable right to a benefit: one that cannot be lost whatever happens or fails to happen.
notes.explanation: A qualified plan must meet a minimum vesting standard for when benefits vest.
notes.example: Like a loyalty bonus that becomes yours for keeps after a set time, even if you leave.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Minimum vesting standard”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: Minimum vesting standard must be met. Your plan must satisfy certain requirements regarding when benefits vest. A benefit is vested (you have a fixed right to it) when it becomes nonforfeitable. A benefit is nonforfeitable if it can't be lost upon the happening, or failure to happen, of any event.

notes.front: For qualified plans, who are the first three kinds of disqualified person in Pub 560’s list?
notes.back: A fiduciary of the plan; a person providing services to the plan; an employer any of whose employees are covered.
notes.explanation: Pub 560’s list continues beyond these three, so there are further ways to be a disqualified person.
notes.example: Like the people standing too close to the plan’s money to trade with it: its trustee, its adviser, the employer.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Disqualified person”, PDF p. 36
notes.evidence: You are a disqualified person if you are any of the following. 1. A fiduciary of the plan. 2. A person providing services to the plan. 3. An employer, any of whose employees are covered by the plan.

notes.front: What does section 409A do to amounts deferred under a nonqualified deferred compensation plan?
notes.back: It makes them currently includible in gross income, with additional taxes, unless its requirements on elections and distributions are met.
notes.explanation: Only amounts not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture and not already included in income are caught.
notes.example: Like an executive’s promise of pay later: if the deferral rules are broken, the pay is taxed now.
notes.source: Publication 15-A (2025), Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide, “Nonqualified Deferred Compensation Plans”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: Section 409A provides that all amounts deferred under a nonqualified deferred compensation (NQDC) plan for all tax years are currently includible in gross income (to the extent the amounts deferred are not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture and not previously included in gross income) and subject to additional taxes

notes.front: What is a patronage dividend from a farm cooperative?
notes.back: A refund-type distribution a cooperative pays to members who buy supplies or sell products through it.
notes.explanation: Pub 225 notes a marketing cooperative may pay either patronage dividends or a per-unit retain certificate.
notes.example: Like a year-end rebate from the farmers’ co-op based on how much feed you bought through it.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Income From Cooperatives”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: If you buy farm supplies through a cooperative, you may receive income from the cooperative in the form of patronage dividends (refunds). If you sell your farm products through a cooperative, you may receive either patronage dividends or a per-unit retain certificate

notes.front: What is farm income averaging on Schedule J?
notes.back: An election to figure this year’s tax by spreading all or part of farming or fishing taxable income over the previous 3 years (base years).
notes.explanation: Only taxable income from a trade or business of farming or fishing can be averaged this way.
notes.example: Like smoothing a bumper harvest year across three leaner years, so less of it falls in the top brackets.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule J (Form 1040) (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Use Schedule J (Form 1040) to elect to figure your 2025 income tax by averaging, over the previous 3 years (base years), all or part of your 2025 taxable income from your trade or business of farming or fishing.

notes.front: What two requirements make a taxpayer a real estate professional for the passive activity rules?
notes.back: Over half of all personal services, and over 750 hours, in real property trades or businesses in which they materially participated.
notes.explanation: Both tests count only real property trades or businesses in which the taxpayer materially participated.
notes.example: Like a full-time property developer rather than a salaried worker with one flat to let.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Real Estate Professional”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: More than half of the personal services you performed in all trades or businesses during the tax year were performed in real property trades or businesses in which you materially participated. • You performed more than 750 hours of services during the tax year in real property trades or businesses

notes.front: What is active participation in a rental real estate activity?
notes.back: A less stringent standard than material participation: for example, making management decisions in a significant and bona fide sense.
notes.explanation: Approving tenants, setting rental terms and approving expenditures are the decisions Pub 925 gives as examples.
notes.example: Like a landlord who uses a letting agent but still approves each new tenant and the rent.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Active participation”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Active participation is a less stringent standard than material participation. For example, you may be treated as actively participating if you make management decisions in a significant and bona fide sense. Management decisions that count as active participation include approving new tenants, deciding on rental terms, approving expenditures

notes.front: What is residential rental property for depreciation?
notes.back: A building or structure, such as a rental home, if 80% or more of its gross rental income for the year is from dwelling units.
notes.explanation: A dwelling unit is a house or apartment used to provide living accommodations.
notes.example: Like a block of flats with one small shop: the flats bring in over 80% of the rent, so the building is residential.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Which Property Class Applies Under GDS?”, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: Residential rental property. This is any building or structure, such as a rental home (including a mobile home), if 80% or more of its gross rental income for the tax year is from dwelling units. A dwelling unit is a house or apartment used to provide living accommodations

notes.front: What is advance rent, and when is it income?
notes.back: Any amount received before the period it covers; it is income in the year received, whatever the period or accounting method.
notes.explanation: Pub 527 makes no exception for accrual-method landlords or for rent covering a later year.
notes.example: Like a tenant paying the last month’s rent on signing: it is taxed when paid, not when that month comes.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Advance rent”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Advance rent is any amount you receive before the period that it covers. Include advance rent in your rental income in the year you receive it regardless of the period covered or the method of accounting you use.

notes.front: Under the SEP eligibility rules, what minimum age may an employer require?
notes.back: Age 21: an employee who has reached 21 (and meets the service and pay tests) is eligible.
notes.explanation: Age is one of three parts of the test; the service and pay parts apply as well.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Eligible employee”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Has reached age 21.

notes.front: Under the SEP eligibility rules, how much prior service may an employer require?
notes.back: Work for the employer in at least 3 of the last 5 years.
notes.explanation: The test counts years with any work, not continuous service.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Eligible employee”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Has worked for you in at least 3 of the last 5 years.

notes.front: For 2025, a SEP may require an eligible employee to have received at least {{c1::$750}} in compensation from the employer.
notes.explanation: The amount is indexed; Pub 560 gives $800 for 2026.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Eligible employee”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Has received at least $750 in compensation from you in 2025. The amount is $800 for 2026.

notes.front: A SEP uses the strictest allowed terms. Dana, aged 24, worked for the firm in 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025 (not 2021 or 2023) and earned $9,000 in 2025. Must she be covered for 2025?
notes.back: Yes: she has reached 21, worked in 3 of the last 5 years, and earned at least $750 in 2025.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No, because her service was not continuous
C) No, because she is under 25
notes.choicesExplained: B: the test is at least 3 of the last 5 years, not consecutive years. C: the age limit is 21.
notes.explanation: Step 1: age 24 ≥ 21. Step 2: she worked in 3 of the 5 years 2020–2024, and in 3 of 2021–2025, so the service test is met however the years are counted. Step 3: $9,000 ≥ $750.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Eligible employee”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Has reached age 21. • Has worked for you in at least 3 of the last 5 years. • Has received at least $750 in compensation from you in 2025.

notes.front: For 2025, contributions to a common-law employee’s SEP IRA can’t exceed the lesser of 25% of the employee’s compensation or {{c1::$70,000}}.
notes.explanation: Both caps apply, and whichever is lower governs.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Contribution Limits”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: Contributions you make for 2025 to a common-law employee's SEP IRA can't exceed the lesser of 25% of the employee's compensation or $70,000.

notes.front: An employee earns $64,000 in 2025. What is the most the employer can contribute to her SEP IRA?
notes.choicesExplained: B: the dollar cap applies only if 25% of pay is higher. C: 20% is the reduced rate for the self-employed owner, not for employees.
notes.explanation: Step 1: 25% × $64,000 = $16,000. Step 2: compare with $70,000; the lesser is $16,000.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Contribution Limits”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: Contributions you make for 2025 to a common-law employee's SEP IRA can't exceed the lesser of 25% of the employee's compensation or $70,000.

notes.front: For 2025, the maximum compensation used for figuring retirement plan contributions and benefits is {{c1::$350,000}}.
notes.explanation: Pay above the limit is ignored when a percentage is applied; the limit rises to $360,000 for 2026.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “What’s New: Compensation limits”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: For 2025, the maximum compensation used for figuring contributions and benefits is $350,000. This limit increases to $360,000 for 2026.

notes.front: An executive earns $420,000 in 2025 and is covered by a SEP paying 25% of pay. What is the maximum contribution for him?
notes.back: $70,000: 25% × $350,000 capped compensation = $87,500, which is over the $70,000 limit.
notes.choicesExplained: B: this ignores the $70,000 limit. C: this uses pay above the $350,000 compensation limit.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “What’s New: Compensation limits”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: For 2025, the maximum compensation used for figuring contributions and benefits is $350,000.

notes.front: A sole proprietor with a 25% SEP plan rate has net earnings from self-employment of $100,000 after deducting half her self-employment tax, but before her own SEP contribution. What is the most she can contribute for herself?
notes.back: $20,000: for the self-employed, the limit is 20% of net earnings from self-employment.
notes.choicesExplained: B: 25% is the rate for common-law employees; the owner’s own rate is reduced. C: $70,000 is the overall dollar cap, far above 20% of her earnings.
notes.explanation: Step 1: because her own contribution is not yet deducted, her rate is 25% ÷ 1.25 = 20%. Step 2: 20% × $100,000 = $20,000, below $70,000, so $20,000 is the limit.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Contribution Limits”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: 25% of the employee's compensation (or, for you, 20% of your net earnings from self-employment). • $70,000.

notes.front: If an employer makes SEP contributions, what must they be based on, and whom must they not favour?
notes.back: A written allocation formula; they must not discriminate in favour of highly compensated employees.
notes.explanation: The formula must be in writing, and the favouring test looks at highly compensated employees as defined in chapter 1 of Pub 560.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Contributions”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: But if you make contributions, they must be based on a written allocation formula and must not discriminate in favor of highly compensated employees (defined in chapter 1).

notes.front: By when must an employer make its SEP contribution for a year?
notes.back: By the due date of the employer’s return, including extensions.
notes.explanation: Pub 560’s table of key rules gives this as the last date for SEP contributions.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Table 1. Key Retirement Plan Rules for 2025”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: SEP Due date of employer's return (including extensions).

notes.front: A calendar-year sole proprietor validly extends his 2025 Form 1040 to 15 October 2026. Can a SEP contribution he makes on 1 October 2026 count for 2025?
notes.back: Yes: SEP contributions may be made up to the due date of the employer’s return, including extensions.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No, the deadline is 31 December 2025
C) No, the deadline is 15 April 2026 regardless of extension
notes.choicesExplained: B: the SEP deadline runs to the return due date, not the year end. C: extensions count for the SEP deadline.
notes.explanation: His extended due date is 15 October 2026, and 1 October 2026 falls before it.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Table 1. Key Retirement Plan Rules for 2025”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: SEP Due date of employer's return (including extensions).

notes.front: For 2025, annual additions to a participant’s defined contribution account can’t exceed the lesser of 100% of compensation or {{c1::$70,000}}.
notes.explanation: Catch-up contributions are not counted towards this limit.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Limits on Contributions and Benefits”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: For 2025, a defined contribution plan's annual contributions and other additions (excluding earnings) to the account of a participant can't exceed the lesser of the following amounts. 1. 100% of the participant's compensation. 2. $70,000 for 2025 ($72,000 for 2026). Catch-up contributions (discussed later under Limit on Elective Deferrals) aren't subject to the above limit.

notes.front: In 2025 a 40-year-old earning $150,000 defers $23,500 to a 401(k); the employer adds $30,000 profit-sharing and $4,000 of forfeitures are allocated to him. Are his annual additions within the limit?
notes.choices:
A) Yes, $57,500
B) No, they exceed $70,000
C) Yes, because forfeitures do not count
notes.choicesExplained: B: the total is $57,500. C: forfeitures allocated to his account are annual additions.
notes.explanation: Step 1: add employee contributions, employer contributions and forfeitures: $57,500. Step 2: limit = lesser of $150,000 or $70,000 = $70,000.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Chapter 1. Definitions: Annual additions”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Annual additions are the total of all your contributions in a year, employee contributions (not including rollovers), and forfeitures allocated to a participant's account.

notes.front: How does the 2025 limit for a defined benefit plan differ from the defined contribution limit?
notes.back: Defined benefit: yearly benefit up to the lesser of 100% of average pay (highest 3 years) or $280,000. Defined contribution: additions up to $70,000.
notes.explanation: One caps what the plan pays out each year; the other caps what goes into the account.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Limits on Contributions and Benefits”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: For 2025, the annual benefit for a participant under a defined benefit plan can't exceed the lesser of the following amounts. 1. 100% of the participant's average compensation for their highest 3 consecutive calendar years. 2. $280,000 for 2025 ($290,000 for 2026).

notes.front: What does a defined contribution plan provide, and what largely drives a participant’s benefit?
notes.back: An individual account for each participant; benefits depend largely on the amount contributed to that account.
notes.explanation: Income, expenses, gains, losses and forfeitures allocated to the account also affect the benefit.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Defined Contribution Plan”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: A defined contribution plan provides an individual account for each participant in the plan. It provides benefits to a participant largely based on the amount contributed to that participant's account. Benefits are also affected by any income, expenses, gains, losses, and forfeitures of other accounts that may be allocated to an account.

notes.front: A plan promises each retiree 1.5% of final pay for each year of service, with the employer paying in whatever an actuary says is needed. Which kind of plan is it?
notes.back: A defined benefit plan: contributions are set by what is needed to provide a definitely determinable benefit.
notes.choices:
A) Defined benefit plan
B) Defined contribution plan
C) SEP
notes.choicesExplained: B: there is no individual account whose balance drives the benefit. C: a SEP pays into employees’ IRAs, with no promised benefit.
notes.explanation: The benefit is fixed by formula and funded actuarially, which is how Pub 560 describes a defined benefit plan.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Defined Benefit Plan”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: Contributions to a defined benefit plan are based on what is needed to provide definitely determinable benefits to plan participants.

notes.front: For 2025, the limit on elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan, other than catch-up contributions, is {{c1::$23,500}}.
notes.explanation: The same limit applies to section 403(b) and 457(b) plans, and it rises to $24,500 for 2026.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “What’s New: Elective deferral limits”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026. These limits apply for participants in SARSEPs, 401(k) plans (excluding SIMPLE plans), section 403(b) plans, and section 457(b) plans.

notes.front: Jorge is 55 at the end of 2025 and in his employer’s 401(k) plan. What is the most he can defer for 2025, including catch-up?
notes.back: $31,000: $23,500 plus the $7,500 catch-up contribution.
notes.choicesExplained: B: leaves out the catch-up available at 50 or over. C: the higher limit applies only to those reaching 60 to 63.
notes.explanation: Step 1: basic limit $23,500. Step 2: add $7,500 catch-up for age 50 or over. $23,500 + $7,500 = $31,000.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Table 1. Key Retirement Plan Rules for 2025”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Elective deferral up to $23,500; $31,000 if age 50 or over (but not attaining age 60, 61, 62, or 63).

notes.front: From 2025, which participants may have a higher catch-up contribution limit under section 109 of the 2022 retirement legislation?
notes.back: Those aged 60 to 63, in most 401(k), 403(b) and other deferred compensation plans that permit it.
notes.explanation: Pub 560 lists this among the 2025 changes to catch-up contributions.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “What’s New: Higher catch-up contribution limit for ages 60 to 63”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Beginning in 2025, section 109 of the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 permits a deferred compensation plan (including most 401(k) and 403(b)

notes.front: For 2025, an employee’s salary reduction contributions to a SIMPLE IRA generally can’t exceed {{c1::$16,500}}.
notes.explanation: The limit is indexed: Pub 560 gives $17,000 for 2026.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Salary reduction contributions”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: The amount the employee chooses to have you contribute to a SIMPLE IRA on their behalf generally can't be more than $16,500 for 2025 and increases to $17,000 for 2026.

notes.front: What must an employer contribute to a SIMPLE IRA plan?
notes.back: Either dollar-for-dollar matching up to 3% of the employee’s compensation, or fixed nonelective contributions of 2% of compensation.
notes.explanation: Higher amounts apply for employers that elect to allow higher salary reduction contributions.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Table 1. Key Retirement Plan Rules for 2025”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Employer contribution: Either dollar-for-dollar matching contributions, up to 3% of employee's compensation,3 or fixed nonelective contributions of 2% of compensation.2 Higher matching and fixed nonelective contributions apply for certain employers who elect to allow higher salary reduction contributions.

notes.front: Under a SIMPLE IRA plan using the 3% match, an employee earning $48,000 defers $6,000 in 2025. What matching contribution must the employer make?
notes.back: $1,440: dollar-for-dollar up to 3% × $48,000.
notes.choicesExplained: B: the match stops at 3% of pay. C: $960 is 2% of pay, the nonelective alternative, not the match.
notes.explanation: Step 1: 3% × $48,000 = $1,440. Step 2: she deferred $6,000, more than $1,440, so the full $1,440 is matched.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Table 1. Key Retirement Plan Rules for 2025”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Either dollar-for-dollar matching contributions, up to 3% of employee's compensation,3 or fixed nonelective contributions of 2% of compensation.

notes.front: Last year a firm had 112 employees, of whom 94 earned $5,000 or more. Can it set up a SIMPLE IRA plan this year (with no other plan)?
notes.back: Yes: the test counts employees who received $5,000 or more, and 94 is 100 or fewer.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No, because it had 112 employees
C) No, because some employees earned under $5,000
notes.choicesExplained: B: only employees paid $5,000 or more are counted. C: lower-paid employees simply do not count towards the 100.
notes.explanation: The limit is 100 or fewer employees who received at least $5,000 of compensation in the preceding year.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Who Can Set up a SIMPLE IRA Plan?”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: SIMPLE IRA plan only if you had 100 or fewer employees who received $5,000 or more in compensation from you for the preceding year.

notes.front: Under a qualified plan, contributions or benefits must not discriminate in favour of {{c1::highly compensated employees}}.
notes.back: Highly compensated employees.
notes.explanation: This is one of the qualification rules a plan must meet to keep its tax benefits.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Qualification Rules”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: Under the plan, contributions or benefits to be provided must not discriminate in favor of highly compensated employees.

notes.front: For the 2025 plan year, which is an HCE: Ana, who owns 6% of the firm and earned $48,000 in 2024, or Ben, who owns nothing and earned $150,000 in 2024?
notes.back: Ana: owning more than 5% makes her an HCE whatever she earns. Ben’s $150,000 is not over the $155,000 figure for 2024.
notes.choices:
A) Ana only
B) Ben only
C) Both
notes.choicesExplained: B: Ben’s 2024 pay did not exceed $155,000. C: only Ana meets either test.
notes.explanation: Step 1: Ana 6% > 5% owner, so HCE. Step 2: Ben $150,000 ≤ $155,000 and no ownership, so not HCE.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Chapter 1. Definitions: Highly compensated employee”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: Owned more than 5% of the interest in your business at any time during the year or the preceding year, regardless of how much compensation that person earned or received

notes.front: To be qualified, how many employees must a defined benefit plan benefit?
notes.back: At least the lesser of 50 employees or the greater of 40% of all employees or two employees (one, if there is only one).
notes.explanation: If there is only one employee, the plan must benefit that employee.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Minimum coverage requirement”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: To be a qualified plan, a defined benefit plan must benefit at least the lesser of the following. 1. 50 employees. 2. The greater of: a. 40% of all employees, or b. Two employees. If there is only one employee, the plan must benefit that employee.

notes.front: At the end of the preceding plan year, key employees held $650,000 of a plan’s $1,000,000 total account balances. Is the plan top-heavy?
notes.back: Yes: key employees hold 65%, more than 60% of the total.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No, the test is more than 75%
C) No, the test uses current-year balances only
notes.choicesExplained: B: the threshold is more than 60%. C: the test uses the preceding plan year.
notes.explanation: Step 1: $650,000 ÷ $1,000,000 = 65%. Step 2: 65% > 60%, so the plan is top-heavy.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Top-heavy plan requirements”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: A plan is top-heavy for a plan year if, for the preceding plan year, the total value of accrued benefits or account balances of key employees is more than 60% of the total value of accrued benefits or account balances of all employees.

notes.front: An employee leaves with $12,000 in her plan account, of which $9,000 is vested. What can she no longer lose?
notes.back: The $9,000 vested part: vested benefits are nonforfeitable, so leaving cannot take them away.
notes.choices:
A) The $9,000 vested part
B) All $12,000
C) Nothing: benefits are lost on leaving
notes.choicesExplained: B: the unvested $3,000 can still be forfeited. C: a vested benefit can’t be lost on any event.
notes.explanation: Step 1: $12,000 − $9,000 = $3,000 unvested. Step 2: the $9,000 vested part is nonforfeitable.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Minimum vesting standard”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: A benefit is nonforfeitable if it can't be lost upon the happening, or failure to happen, of any event.

notes.front: What are two kinds of transaction Pub 560 lists as prohibited transactions?
notes.back: A transfer of plan assets to, or use by, a disqualified person; and a fiduciary dealing with plan assets in their own interest.
notes.explanation: These are the first two items of the list of transactions that prohibited transactions generally include.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Prohibited Transactions”, PDF p. 35
notes.evidence: 1. A transfer of plan income or assets to, or use of them by or for the benefit of, a disqualified person. 2. Any act of a fiduciary by which they deal with plan income or assets in the fiduciary's own interest.

notes.front: A business owner, a fiduciary of his company’s 401(k) plan, has the plan buy a building from him for $400,000. What is the problem, and what is the initial tax if it runs for one year?
notes.back: A prohibited transaction with a disqualified person; initial tax 15% × $400,000 = $60,000 for the year.
notes.choices:
A) Prohibited transaction; $60,000
B) None, if the price is fair
C) Prohibited transaction; $400,000
notes.choicesExplained: B: a sale between the plan and a disqualified person is prohibited whatever the price. C: 100% applies only if the transaction isn’t corrected within the tax period.
notes.explanation: Step 1: he is a fiduciary, so a disqualified person. Step 2: 15% × $400,000 × 1 year = $60,000.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Tax on Prohibited Transactions”, PDF p. 36
notes.evidence: The initial tax on a prohibited transaction is 15% of the amount involved for each year (or part of a year) in the tax period. If the transaction isn't corrected within the tax period, an additional tax of 100% of the amount involved is imposed.

notes.front: By when must a plan’s annual return/report (Form 5500 series) generally be filed?
notes.back: By the last day of the seventh month after the plan year ends.
notes.explanation: Pub 560 then lists the forms in the series, including a simplified one for small plans, so the right one can be chosen.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Reporting Requirements”, PDF p. 37
notes.evidence: You may have to file an annual return/report by the last day of the seventh month after the plan year ends.

notes.front: A calendar-year plan must file an annual return/report for 2025. By when is it due, before any extension?
notes.back: 31 July 2026: the last day of the seventh month after the plan year ends.
notes.choices:
A) 31 July 2026
B) 15 April 2026
C) 15 October 2026
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is an individual income tax date, not the plan return date. C: that is the extended individual due date.
notes.explanation: Seven months after December is July, and the last day of July is the 31st.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Reporting Requirements”, PDF p. 37
notes.evidence: You may have to file an annual return/report by the last day of the seventh month after the plan year ends.

notes.front: A sole proprietor’s one-participant plan had total assets of $210,000 at the end of 2025. Must she file Form 5500-EZ for 2025?
notes.back: No: a one-participant plan with total assets of $250,000 or less at year end need not file (except for its final plan year).
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, every plan files each year
C) Yes, because she is self-employed
notes.choicesExplained: B: the $250,000 exception removes the duty for small one-participant plans. C: self-employment does not change the asset test.
notes.explanation: $210,000 is not more than $250,000, so the filing is not required, though every plan should file for its final year.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Form 5500-EZ not required”, PDF p. 37
notes.evidence: If your one-participant plan (or plans) had total assets of $250,000 or less at the end of the plan year, then you don't have to file Form 5500-EZ for that plan year. All plans should file a Form 5500-EZ for the final plan year

notes.front: How does a SEP, SIMPLE or qualified plan differ from a nonqualified deferred compensation plan in its tax treatment?
notes.back: Plan contributions are deductible and earnings generally tax free until distributed; nonqualified deferrals can be taxed at once if section 409A is not met.
notes.explanation: Pub 560 describes the tax-favoured plans; the section 409A rule for nonqualified plans comes from Pub 15-A.
notes.source: Publication 560 (2025), Retirement Plans for Small Business, “Introduction”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: SEP, SIMPLE, and qualified plans offer you and your employees a tax-favored way to save for retirement. You can deduct contributions you make to the plan for your employees.

notes.front: What is Schedule F (Form 1040) used for, and with which returns may it be filed?
notes.back: To report farm income and expenses; it may be filed with Form 1040, and also with Forms 1041 and 1065, among others.
notes.explanation: The Schedule F instructions list individual, estate and trust, and partnership returns it can accompany.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule F (Form 1040) (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Use Schedule F (Form 1040) to report farm income and expenses. File it with Form 1040, 1040-SR, 1040-SS, 1040-NR, 1041, or 1065.

notes.front: A partnership runs a dairy farm. On which schedule does it report the farm income and expenses, filed with which return?
notes.back: Schedule F (Form 1040), filed with the partnership’s Form 1065.
notes.choices:
A) Schedule F with Form 1065
B) Form 4835 with Form 1065
C) Schedule C with Form 1065
notes.choicesExplained: B: Form 4835 is for landlords who do not materially participate. C: Schedule C is not the farm schedule.
notes.explanation: The Schedule F instructions list Form 1065 among the returns Schedule F may be filed with.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule F (Form 1040) (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Use Schedule F (Form 1040) to report farm income and expenses. File it with Form 1040, 1040-SR, 1040-SS, 1040-NR, 1041, or 1065.

notes.front: A farmer generally reports patronage dividends as income on Schedule F for {{c1::the tax year received}}.
notes.back: The tax year received.
notes.explanation: They include cash, the stated dollar value of qualified written notices of allocation, and the fair market value of other property.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Patronage Dividends”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: You generally report patronage dividends as income on Schedule F for the tax year you receive them. They include the following items. • Money paid as a patronage dividend, including cash advances received (for example, from a marketing cooperative). • The stated dollar value of qualified written notices of allocation. • The fair market value of other property.

notes.front: A farmer receives two patronage dividends: $600 on fertiliser bought for the farm, and $200 on a family car bought through the co-op. How much is income?
notes.back: $600. The $200 on a personal purchase is not income; it reduces the car’s basis instead.
notes.choices:
A) $600
B) $800
C) Nothing until the cash is spent
notes.choicesExplained: B: dividends on non-deductible personal purchases are not income. C: patronage dividends are income in the year received.
notes.explanation: Step 1: fertiliser is a deductible farm expense, so its $600 dividend is income. Step 2: the car is a personal item, so its $200 reduces basis.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Patronage Dividends”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: Don't report as income any patronage dividends you receive from expenditures that weren't deductible, such as buying personal or family items, capital assets, or depreciable property. You must reduce the cost or other basis of these items by the amount of such patronage dividends received.

notes.front: Must a farmer include crop insurance proceeds received for physical crop damage in income?
notes.back: Yes. Proceeds for physical damage or reduced crop revenue are income, generally in the year received.
notes.explanation: Pub 225 also treats livestock insurance plans as crop insurance.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Crop Insurance and Crop Disaster Payments”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: You must include in income any crop insurance proceeds you receive as the result of physical crop damage or reduction of crop revenue, or both. Livestock insurance plans, such as livestock gross margin (LGM) and livestock risk protection (LRP) are also considered crop insurance. You generally include them in the year you receive them.

notes.front: A cash-method farmer’s corn is hailed out in August 2025 and she receives $40,000 of insurance in October 2025. She normally sells over 60% of her corn in the following year. Can she report the $40,000 in 2026?
notes.back: Yes, by election: she uses the cash method, got the proceeds in the damage year, and normally reports over 50% of such income later.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, by election
B) No, insurance is always income when received
C) Only if she uses an accrual method
notes.choicesExplained: B: Pub 225 allows postponement when the conditions are met. C: the election requires the cash method.
notes.explanation: All three conditions in Pub 225 are met, so the proceeds can be reported in the year after the damage.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Election to postpone reporting until the following year”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: You can postpone reporting eligible crop insurance proceeds as income until the year following the year the physical damage occurred if you meet all the following conditions. • You use the cash method of accounting. • You receive the crop insurance proceeds in the same tax year the crops are damaged.

notes.front: Besides the area being designated for federal assistance, what are three conditions for postponing gain on extra livestock sold because of weather?
notes.back: Farming is the principal business; the cash method is used; and the extra animals would not have been sold but for the weather.
notes.explanation: Each condition must be met; the designation of the area is a further one.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Sales Caused by Weather-Related Conditions”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: Your principal trade or business is farming. • You use the cash method of accounting. • You can show that, under your usual business practices, you wouldn't have sold or exchanged the additional animals this year except for the weather-related condition.

notes.front: Drought in a federally designated area forces a cash-method rancher, who usually sells 80 steers a year, to sell 110 in 2025. For how many can he postpone reporting the gain until 2026?
notes.back: 30: only the additional animals sold because of the weather, 110 − 80.
notes.choices:
A) 30
B) 110
C) None
notes.choicesExplained: B: the animals he normally sells are reported as usual. C: he meets the conditions for the extra animals.
notes.explanation: Step 1: normal sales 80. Step 2: 110 − 80 = 30 additional animals whose gain may be postponed.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Sales Caused by Weather-Related Conditions”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: If you sell or exchange more livestock, including poultry, than you normally would in a year because of a drought, flood, or other

notes.front: A farmer sold extra cattle in May 2025 because of flooding; the area was declared eligible for federal assistance in July 2025 because of the same flooding. Does the sale qualify?
notes.back: Yes: a sale before designation qualifies if the same weather condition caused the designation.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No, the sale came before the designation
C) Only if the designation was by the President
notes.choicesExplained: B: Pub 225 expressly allows sales made before the area became eligible. C: designation can also come from the Department of Agriculture or other federal agencies.
notes.explanation: Pub 225 looks at the cause: the same flooding led to both the sale and the designation.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Sales Caused by Weather-Related Conditions”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: Sales or exchanges made before an area became eligible for federal assistance qualify if the weather-related condition that caused the sale or exchange also caused the area to be designated as eligible for federal assistance.

notes.front: A farmer pledges wheat to secure a $50,000 Market Assistance Loan from the Commodity Credit Corporation. Is the loan income?
notes.back: Generally not, but he may choose to treat it as a sale and report the $50,000 as income in the year received.
notes.choices:
A) Not generally, but he may elect to report it
B) Always income when received
C) Never income, even if forfeited
notes.choicesExplained: B: loans are generally not income. C: forfeiting pledged crops in full payment is treated as a sale.
notes.explanation: Pub 225 lets a farmer who pledges production treat the loan as though the crop had been sold.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Market Assistance Loans (MALs)”, PDF p. 12
notes.evidence: Generally, you don't report loans you receive as income. However, if you pledge part or all of your production to secure a MAL, you can treat the loan as if it were a sale of the crop and report the loan proceeds as income in the year you receive them.

notes.front: Can a farmer exclude payments received under cost-sharing conservation programmes?
notes.back: Part or all of a payment under certain federal or state cost-sharing conservation, reclamation and restoration programmes can be excluded.
notes.explanation: Pub 225 points to separate effects of the exclusion that must also be considered.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Cost-Sharing Exclusion (Improvements)”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: You can exclude from your income part or all of a payment you receive under certain federal or state cost-sharing conservation, reclamation, and restoration programs. However, see Effects of the exclusion, later.

notes.front: A cash-method farmer with no exception pays $30,000 in December 2025 for feed and seed to use in 2026. Her other deductible farm expenses for 2025 are $50,000. How much of the prepayment can she deduct in 2025?
notes.back: $25,000: 50% of her other deductible farm expenses ($50,000).
notes.choicesExplained: B: the prepayment exceeds the 50% limit. C: the limit is 50% of other farm expenses, not of the prepayment.
notes.explanation: Step 1: 50% × $50,000 = $25,000 limit. Step 2: $30,000 exceeds it, so only $25,000 is deducted in 2025.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Prepaid Farm Supplies”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: your deduction for prepaid farm supplies in the year you pay for them may be limited to 50% of your other deductible farm expenses for the year

notes.front: A farmer has gross income from farming of $40,000 and $12,000 of deductible soil and water conservation expenses. How much can he deduct this year?
notes.back: $10,000: 25% of $40,000; the $2,000 excess carries over.
notes.choicesExplained: B: the deduction is capped at 25% of gross income from farming. C: 25% is applied to gross income, not to the expenses.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Soil and Water Conservation Expenses: Carryover of deduction”, PDF p. 32
notes.evidence: If your deductible conservation expenses in any year are more than 25% of your gross income from farming for that year, you can carry the unused deduction over to later years.

notes.front: A farmer places a new 7-year tractor and a 15-year farm building improvement in service in 2025. Which must use the 150% declining balance method (unless straight line is elected)?
notes.back: The 15-year property. For 3-, 5-, 7- and 10-year farm property placed in service after 2017, 150% is no longer required.
notes.choices:
A) The 15-year property only
B) Both
C) The tractor only
notes.choicesExplained: B: the 150% requirement was dropped for 7-year farm property after 2017. C: it is the reverse; 15- and 20-year property still uses 150% or a straight line election.
notes.explanation: Pub 225 lets 3- to 10-year farm property use other methods, but keeps 150% (or a straight line election) for 15- and 20-year property.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Table 7-1 notes: Property used in farming business”, PDF p. 47
notes.evidence: For 3-, 5-, 7-, or 10-year property used in a farming business and placed in service after 2017, the 150% declining balance method is no longer required, but may be elected. However, for 15- or 20-year property placed in service in a farming business, you must use the 150% declining balance method

notes.front: Who uses Form 4835?
notes.back: A landowner or sub-lessor who did not materially participate in the farm, to report rental income based on crops or livestock produced by the tenant.
notes.explanation: Material participation here is judged for self-employment tax purposes, as the form says.
notes.source: Form 4835 (2025), Farm Rental Income and Expenses, “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: If you were the landowner (or sub-lessor) and did not materially participate (for self-employment tax purposes) in the operation or management of the farm, use Form 4835 to report farm rental income based on crops or livestock produced by the tenant.

notes.front: Ruth rents her farmland to a tenant for a third of the crop. She does not take part in running the farm. Where does she report the crop-share income, and is it self-employment income?
notes.back: On Form 4835 (net carried to Schedule E); it is not self-employment income because she does not materially participate.
notes.choices:
A) Form 4835; not self-employment income
B) Schedule F; self-employment income
C) Form 4835; self-employment income
notes.choicesExplained: B: Schedule F is for landlords who materially participate. C: without material participation, crop shares aren’t self-employment income.
notes.explanation: Pub 225 sends a non-participating landlord’s crop shares to Form 4835 and keeps them out of self-employment income.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Rents (Including Crop Shares)”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: You don't materially participate in operating the farm. Report this income on Form 4835, and carry the net income or loss to Schedule E (Form 1040), page 2.

notes.front: In Pub 225’s landlord material participation test, what share of the tools, equipment and livestock used in production must the landlord furnish for that action to count?
notes.back: At least half.
notes.explanation: Supplying at least half of the means of production is one of the actions Pub 225 lists for landlords.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Landlord Participation in Farming”, PDF p. 80
notes.evidence: Furnish at least half the tools, equipment, and livestock used in the production activities.

notes.front: Ivy began farming in 2025 after years as a teacher and had a bumper first harvest. Can she use Schedule J to average her 2025 farm income?
notes.back: Yes: she need not have farmed in the base years to make the election.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No, she must have farmed in all 3 base years
C) No, averaging is only for fishing income
notes.choicesExplained: B: the instructions say no farming is required in the base years. C: it applies to farming or fishing income.
notes.explanation: The election may help most when this year’s farm income is high and earlier years’ taxable income was low, as here.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule J (Form 1040) (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: In order to qualify for this election, you aren't required to have been in the business of farming or fishing during any of the base years.

notes.front: Does the farm income averaging election apply when figuring alternative minimum tax?
notes.back: No: the election doesn’t apply when figuring alternative minimum tax on Form 6251.
notes.explanation: Form 6251 is completed without the averaging election.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule J (Form 1040) (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: This election doesn't apply when figuring your alternative minimum tax on Form 6251.

notes.front: A farmer’s 2025 gross farm income is $9,300 and actual farm net earnings are $7,000. Under the farm optional method, what are her farm net earnings for SE tax?
notes.back: $6,200: two-thirds of $9,300, since gross farm income is $10,860 or less.
notes.choicesExplained: B: $7,240 applies only when gross farm income is more than $10,860. C: that is her actual figure; the optional method gives two-thirds of gross.
notes.explanation: Step 1: $9,300 ≤ $10,860. Step 2: 2/3 × $9,300 = $6,200, which is less than her actual $7,000.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Farm Optional Method”, PDF p. 82
notes.evidence: IF your gross farm income is... THEN your net earnings are equal to... $10,860 or less two-thirds of your gross farm income. more than $10,860 $7,240.

notes.front: A landlord gives crop shares she received to a charity before selling them. Must she report them?
notes.back: Yes: crop shares a landlord gives away are treated as converted to money when given, so their fair market value is income.
notes.explanation: Pub 225 applies this even to gifts to a qualified charitable organisation.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Crop shares you give to others (gift)”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: Crop shares you receive as a landlord and give to others are considered converted to money when you make the gift. You must report the fair market value of the crop share as income, even though someone else receives payment for the crop share. This applies even if the gift is made to a qualified charitable organization.

notes.front: At least two-thirds of a farmer’s gross income for 2025 is from farming. How can he avoid making any 2025 estimated tax payments?
notes.back: File his 2025 Form 1040 and pay all the tax due by 2 March 2026.
notes.choices:
A) File and pay in full by 2 March 2026
B) Pay by 15 April 2026
C) He can’t: farmers pay quarterly like others
notes.choicesExplained: B: 15 April is too late for the farmer rule. C: Pub 225 gives qualifying farmers this special rule.
notes.explanation: Pub 225 lets farmers with two-thirds of gross income from farming skip estimated tax if they file and pay by 2 March.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Estimated Tax”, PDF p. 78
notes.evidence: if at least two-thirds of your gross income for 2024 or 2025 is from farming and you file your 2025 Form 1040 and pay all the tax due by March 2, 2026, you don't have to make any estimated tax payments for 2025.

notes.front: A qualifying farmer who will not file and pay in full by 2 March 2026 must pay the required annual estimated tax payment by {{c1::15 January 2026}}.
notes.back: 15 January 2026.
notes.explanation: The flowchart treats this single January payment as the farmer’s required annual payment.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer’s Tax Guide, “Estimated tax for farmers flowchart”, PDF p. 92
notes.evidence: You must pay your estimated tax (your required annual payment) by January 15, 2026.

notes.front: For a real estate professional, how are rental real estate activities in which she materially participated treated?
notes.back: They aren’t passive activities; the income or losses are reported as nonpassive.
notes.explanation: The rule applies only to the rental activities in which the professional materially participated.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Activities That Aren’t Passive Activities”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: if you qualified as a real estate professional, rental real estate activities in which you materially participated aren't passive activities.

notes.front: Omar works 1,800 hours a year as a salaried engineer and spends 800 hours managing his rental buildings, in which he materially participates. Is he a real estate professional?
notes.back: No: 800 hours is over 750, but it is not more than half of his 2,600 total hours of personal services.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, because he exceeds 750 hours
C) Yes, because he materially participates
notes.choicesExplained: B: both tests must be met; the half-of-services test fails. C: material participation alone is not enough.
notes.explanation: Step 1: 800 > 750 passes. Step 2: 800 ÷ (1,800 + 800) = 31%, not more than half, so he fails.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Real Estate Professional”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: You qualified as a real estate professional for the year if you met both of the following requirements. • More than half of the personal services you performed in all trades or businesses during the tax year were performed in real property trades or businesses in which you materially participated.

notes.front: Do hours worked as an employee in a real property business count towards the real estate professional tests?
notes.back: Not unless the taxpayer was a 5% owner of the employer.
notes.explanation: A 5% owner is someone owning more than 5% of the employer’s stock or capital or profits interest.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Real Estate Professional”, PDF p. 9
notes.evidence: Don't count personal services you performed as an employee in real property trades or businesses unless you were a 5% owner of your employer. You were a 5% owner if you owned (or are considered to have owned) more than 5% of your employer's outstanding stock, outstanding voting stock, or capital or profits interest.

notes.front: If you or your spouse actively participated in a passive rental real estate activity, you can deduct up to {{c1::$25,000}} of loss from it against nonpassive income.
notes.explanation: This special allowance is an exception to the general rule disallowing passive activity losses.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Special $25,000 allowance”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: If you or your spouse actively participated in a passive rental real estate activity, the amount of the passive activity loss that is disallowed is decreased and you therefore can deduct up to $25,000 of loss from the activity from your nonpassive income. This special allowance is an exception to the general rule disallowing the passive activity loss.

notes.front: How is the $25,000 special allowance reduced as modified adjusted gross income rises (not married filing separately)?
notes.back: By 50% of MAGI over $100,000; at $150,000 or more it is gone.
notes.explanation: Half of each dollar over $100,000 is lost, so $50,000 of excess uses up the whole allowance.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Modified adjusted gross income limit”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: is reduced by 50% of the amount of your modified adjusted gross income that is more than $100,000 ($50,000 if you're married filing separately). If your modified adjusted gross income is $150,000 or more ($75,000 or more if you're married filing separately), you generally can't use the special allowance.

notes.front: A single landlord who actively participates has a $22,000 rental loss and MAGI of $124,000. How much of the loss can she deduct against nonpassive income?
notes.choicesExplained: B: the allowance is reduced for MAGI over $100,000. C: that subtracts the full $24,000 excess instead of half of it.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Modified adjusted gross income limit”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: is reduced by 50% of the amount of your modified adjusted gross income that is more than $100,000

notes.front: A landlord with MAGI of $180,000 has a $30,000 rental loss. Which status could let her deduct it against salary: the $25,000 allowance or real estate professional status?
notes.back: Only real estate professional status (with material participation); the $25,000 allowance is gone at MAGI of $150,000 or more.
notes.choices:
A) Real estate professional status
B) The $25,000 allowance
C) Either one
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: at $180,000 of MAGI the special allowance is reduced to nothing.
notes.explanation: The allowance depends on MAGI; the real estate professional test depends on hours and share of services, not income.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Modified adjusted gross income limit”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: If your modified adjusted gross income is $150,000 or more ($75,000 or more if you're married filing separately), you generally can't use the special allowance.

notes.front: A doctor owns 5% of a rental building with investors and approves tenants as a committee member. Is she actively participating for the $25,000 allowance?
notes.back: No: an interest of less than 10% (by value) of all interests means she is not treated as actively participating.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, because she makes management decisions
C) Yes, because she is a co-owner
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: without at least a 10% interest, active participation is not available.
notes.explanation: Pub 925 requires the taxpayer’s interest (with a spouse’s) to be at least 10% throughout the year; 5% falls short.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Active participation”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: aren't treated as actively participating in a rental real estate activity unless your interest in the activity (including your spouse's interest) was at least 10% (by value) of all interests in the activity throughout the year.

notes.front: How does active participation compare with material participation?
notes.back: It is a less stringent standard: management decisions made in a significant and bona fide sense can be enough.
notes.explanation: Pub 925 says expressly that the two are not the same.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Active participation”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Active participation isn't the same as material participation (defined later). Active participation is a less stringent standard than material participation.

notes.front: Under the general depreciation system, over how many years are residential rental property and nonresidential real property depreciated?
notes.back: Residential rental property: 27.5 years. Nonresidential real property: 39 years.
notes.explanation: The longer 39-year period applies to real property that is not residential rental property.
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Table 4-1. Recovery periods”, PDF p. 33
notes.evidence: Residential rental property . . . . . . Nonresidential real property . . . . . 25 years3 27.5 years 39 years4

notes.front: A building earns $170,000 of rent from flats and $30,000 from a ground-floor shop. Is it residential rental property?
notes.back: Yes: $170,000 ÷ $200,000 = 85% of gross rental income comes from dwelling units, which is 80% or more.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, 85% from dwelling units
B) No, any commercial tenant makes it nonresidential
C) No, 85% is below the test
notes.choicesExplained: B: the test is a percentage of rent, not an all-or-nothing rule. C: the threshold is 80%.
notes.explanation: Step 1: total rent $200,000. Step 2: $170,000 ÷ $200,000 = 85% ≥ 80%, so it is residential rental property (27.5 years).
notes.source: Publication 946 (2025), How To Depreciate Property, “Which Property Class Applies Under GDS?”, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: if 80% or more of its gross rental income for the tax year is from dwelling units.

notes.front: You use a dwelling unit as a home if you use it for personal purposes for more than the greater of 14 days or {{c1::10% of the days it is rented at a fair rental price}}.
notes.back: 10% of the days rented at a fair rental price.
notes.explanation: Which figure applies depends on how many days the unit is rented: more rental days raise the 10% figure above 14.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Dwelling Unit Used as a Home”, PDF p. 26
notes.evidence: You use a dwelling unit as a home during the tax year if you use it for personal purposes more than the greater of: 1. 14 days, or 2. 10% of the total days it is rented to others at a fair rental price.

notes.front: A beach house is rented at a fair price for 230 days in 2025, and the owners use it themselves for 21 days. Is it used as a home?
notes.back: No: the limit is the greater of 14 days or 23 days (10% × 230), and 21 days is not more than 23.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, because 21 is more than 14
C) Yes, because any personal use counts
notes.choicesExplained: B: the greater of the two figures applies, here 23 days. C: only personal use above the limit makes it a home.
notes.explanation: Step 1: 10% × 230 = 23 days. Step 2: the greater of 14 and 23 is 23. Step 3: 21 ≤ 23, so it is not used as a home.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Dwelling Unit Used as a Home”, PDF p. 26
notes.evidence: You use a dwelling unit as a home during the tax year if you use it for personal purposes more than the greater of: 1. 14 days, or 2. 10% of the total days it is rented to others at a fair rental price.

notes.front: A family lives in its home all year but rents it for 12 days during a golf tournament for $9,000. How is the rent treated?
notes.back: Not reported: a home rented under 15 days isn’t treated as a rental, so its rental income and expenses are left out.
notes.choices:
A) Not reported
B) All $9,000 on Schedule E
C) Reported, with a deduction for 12/365 of all home costs
notes.choicesExplained: B: rentals under 15 days of a home aren’t reported on Schedule E. C: rental expenses for such a period aren’t deducted either.
notes.explanation: Pub 527 says the primary function isn’t rental when a home is rented for less than 15 days.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Used as a home but rented less than 15 days”, PDF p. 28
notes.evidence: If you use a dwelling unit as a home and you rent it less than 15 days during the year, its primary function isn't considered to be rental and it shouldn't be reported on Schedule E (Form 1040). You aren't required to report the rental income and rental expenses from this activity.

notes.front: A cabin was used 200 days in 2025: rented at a fair price for 150 days and used personally for 50. Its total expenses were $16,000. What is the most that can be treated as rental expense?
notes.choicesExplained: B: personal-use days must be taken out. C: that divides by 365 days; the denominator is days the unit was used.
notes.explanation: Step 1: fraction = 150 rental days ÷ 200 days used = 75%. Step 2: 75% × $16,000 = $12,000.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Dividing Expenses”, PDF p. 25
notes.evidence: your rental expenses will be no more than your total expenses multiplied by a fraction, the denominator of which is the total number of days the dwelling unit is used and the numerator of which is the total number of days actually rented at a fair rental price.

notes.front: An accrual-method landlord signs a lease on 1 December 2025 and receives $1,800 for December plus $1,800 as the last month’s rent of the two-year lease. How much is 2025 rental income?
notes.back: $3,600: both payments are received in 2025, and advance rent is income when received, whatever the method.
notes.choicesExplained: B: the last month’s rent is advance rent, taxable when received. C: the accounting method does not spread advance rent.
notes.explanation: Step 1: December rent $1,800. Step 2: last month’s rent $1,800 is advance rent. Total $3,600 in 2025.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Advance rent”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Include advance rent in your rental income in the year you receive it regardless of the period covered or the method of accounting you use.

notes.front: When is a security deposit income to a landlord?
notes.back: Not when received if it is to be returned; only the part kept when the tenant breaks the lease, in the year kept.
notes.explanation: What matters is whether the landlord plans to return the deposit, and then whether any of it is kept.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Security deposits”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: if you plan to return it to your tenant at the end of the lease. But if you keep part or all of the security deposit during any year because your tenant doesn't live up to the terms of the lease, include the amount you keep in your income in that year.

notes.front: In 2024 a landlord received a $2,000 deposit, refundable at lease end. In 2025 the tenant leaves early and damage-free; the landlord keeps $700 for unpaid rent under the lease and refunds $1,300. What is income, and when?
notes.back: $700 in 2025, the year it is kept; nothing in 2024.
notes.choices:
A) $700 in 2025
B) $2,000 in 2024
C) Nothing, because it was called a deposit
notes.choicesExplained: B: a deposit to be returned isn’t income when received. C: the part kept because the tenant broke the lease is income.
notes.explanation: Step 1: 2024, refundable deposit, not income. Step 2: 2025, $2,000 − $1,300 refunded = $700 kept, income in 2025.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Security deposits”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: But if you keep part or all of the security deposit during any year because your tenant doesn't live up to the terms of the lease, include the amount you keep in your income in that year.

notes.front: If property isn’t rented to make a profit, how are the rental income and expenses treated?
notes.back: The rental income must still be reported, but rental expenses can no longer be deducted.
notes.explanation: Pub 527 sends not-for-profit rental income to Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8j.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Not Rented for Profit”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: If you don't rent your property to make a profit, you must still report your rental income, however, you can no longer deduct rental expenses. Where to report. Report your not-for-profit rental income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8j.

notes.front: A client lets a cottage to her brother at a nominal rent, with no profit motive: $3,000 of rent and $5,000 of rental expenses in 2025. How is it reported?
notes.back: The $3,000 is reported as income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8j; the rental expenses can’t be deducted as rental expenses.
notes.choices:
A) $3,000 income; no rental expense deduction
B) A $2,000 rental loss on Schedule E
C) Nothing, as there is no profit
notes.choicesExplained: B: property not rented for profit gets no rental expense deduction. C: the rental income must still be reported.
notes.explanation: Pub 527 requires not-for-profit rental income to be reported while disallowing rental expense deductions.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Not Rented for Profit”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: If you don't rent your property to make a profit, you must still report your rental income, however, you can no longer deduct rental expenses.

notes.front: A landlord spends $600 fixing a leaking tap and $14,000 converting a garage into a studio flat. Which must be capitalised?
notes.back: The $14,000 conversion: it adapts the property to a new use. The $600 repair can be deducted.
notes.choices:
A) Only the $14,000 conversion
B) Both
C) Neither
notes.choicesExplained: B: a repair that is not an improvement may be deducted. C: an expense that adapts property to a new use is an improvement and must be capitalised.
notes.explanation: Pub 527 treats as improvements expenses that result in a betterment, restore the property, or adapt it to a new or different use.
notes.source: Publication 527 (2025), Residential Rental Property, “Repairs and Improvements”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: You must capitalize any expense you pay to improve your rental property. An expense is for an improvement if it results in a betterment to your property, restores your property, or adapts your property to a new or different use.
